analysis.one_liner: Raises the minimum insurance trucking companies must carry from $750,000 to $5 million per crash.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2026 with six Democratic sponsors and has not moved since being referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires trucks carrying freight to hold a minimum of $750,000 in liability insurance, a figure set in 1980 and never raised. This bill would raise that minimum to $5 million and require the Transportation Department to adjust it every five years to keep up with rising medical costs. The purpose is to make sure people seriously hurt or killed in truck crashes can actually collect the compensation they are owed, instead of running out of coverage partway through their medical bills. It was introduced by Rep. Chuy García with five Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured or killed in crashes with commercial trucks, and their families. A victim whose medical bills, lost earnings, and long-term care exceed the current $750,000 minimum — which is common in catastrophic truck crashes — would be able to recover full compensation up to $5 million. Families of those killed would similarly have a far larger pool to draw from. Drivers who share the road with trucks also benefit indirectly, because carriers facing much larger potential payouts have a stronger financial reason to maintain equipment and hire safely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Truck crash victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: It raises the minimum insurance a property-carrying truck must carry from $750,000 to $5 million per occurrence, so a seriously injured victim is far less likely to exhaust the policy before their medical bills, lost wages, and long-term care are covered.

It requires the Secretary of Transportation, working with the Bureau of Labor Statistics, to adjust the minimum every five years for medical-cost inflation, ending the freeze that has kept the level unchanged since 1980.

The findings section documents that $750,000 from 1980 would need to be about $5.8 million in 2025 dollars to keep pace with medical costs, making the case that the current minimum leaves crash victims undercompensated.
Higher required coverage gives trucking companies a stronger financial incentive to operate safely, the same rationale Congress gave when it set the original levels in the Motor Carrier Act of 1980.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and their insurers, who would have to carry roughly six times more liability coverage. Carriers would face higher premiums, and some of that cost would likely be passed through to shipping prices and, eventually, consumer goods. Small carriers with thin margins would feel the squeeze most. Insurers collect larger premiums but also pay larger claims.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings put the inflation-adjusted value of the current $750,000 minimum at about $5.8 million in 2025, meaning the industry has carried less real coverage every year for more than four decades; the costs to insurers and carriers of suddenly making that up would be passed partly into freight rates and consumer prices.

Raising minimum coverage roughly sixfold could raise premiums sharply for small and marginal trucking companies, and the bill does not include a phase-in by carrier size or any relief for small fleets.
As a backbench bill with six sponsors and no committee action, it has no identified vehicle to become law in the current Congress, so its benefits are entirely prospective.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — crash victims actually being made whole instead of undercompensated when a truck destroys a family's finances — is substantial and long overdue by the bill's own inflation math. The cost is real but modest in context: higher insurance premiums for trucking companies, some share of which would flow into freight prices, and potentially more pressure on small carriers. The bill could have been designed with phase-ins by fleet size to soften that, but the five-year effective window already gives the industry time to adjust. On balance the benefits to ordinary people clearly outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 9, 2026, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure; no further action appears in the record.
It has no committee markings, no floor action, and no vote; it sits where most bills without leadership backing sit.
Support is limited to the sponsor and five Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican support recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position; trucking carriers and their insurers keep operating under the 1980-era minimum, and crash victims keep absorbing losses above it. If the bill dies quietly, the carriers are the beneficiaries.

for.name: Rep. Jesús G. "Chuy" García
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise trucking's minimum insurance to $5 million and index it to medical inflation.

for.name: 5 of 217 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Reps. Tran, Huffman, Garamendi, Cohen, Johnson of Georgia)

against.name: American Trucking Associations
against.what_they_did: Has long opposed raising the federal minimum insurance requirement for motor carriers, arguing it would raise premiums and burden small carriers; the industry has successfully kept the 1980 level in place for over four decades.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors are Democrats and there has been no committee or floor vote, so no partisan split has been recorded.

industries.note: Carriers would have to buy roughly six times more liability coverage than the minimum set in 1980, raising their insurance costs; those costs would fall partly on shipping prices. The bill's findings argue the higher requirement also pushes carriers toward safer operations.

Insurers would sell far larger mandatory policies to every property-carrying truck in the country. Insurers profit from the mandate even as they pay bigger claims, so their interest here is not aligned with trucking's.
A larger pool of mandatory coverage means seriously injured victims can actually be compensated rather than recovering a fraction of their losses from a too-small policy.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat untouched in the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee since April 2026, with six sponsors and no Republican support, in a Congress that ends in January 2027. Unless the committee schedules action or the bill attracts many more cosponsors in the remaining months, its most likely path is expiring without a vote.
